--- title: "Choosing the number of clusters" description: "Two measures of how well stations are grouped, the within-cluster sum of squares and the silhouette width, and a baseline from shuffled data that shows which number of clusters stands out." order: 2 categories: [unsupervised] --- ## The number of groups is a choice [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) set $k$ to 2 and found the two kinds of seabed. k-means would have returned three groups as readily, or nine, so the number of habitat types in a survey is first of all a choice. This page shows two measures that help make it, and a simple baseline that turns each measure into a clear answer: run the same clustering on the data with its groups shuffled away, and see which $k$ stands furthest above it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea The first measure is the **within-cluster sum of squares** from [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd): how far stations sit from the centre of their own cluster, squared and added up. It always falls as $k$ rises, because more centres always sit closer to the stations. The classic **elbow** method plots it against $k$ and looks for the bend where adding clusters stops helping much. The second is the **silhouette width**. For each station, compare the average distance to the other stations in its own cluster with the average distance to the stations of the nearest other cluster. A station well inside its own cluster scores close to 1, a station on the border between two scores close to 0, and a station nearer another cluster than its own scores below 0. The average over all stations summarises the whole clustering, and the $k$ with the highest average is the best separated. Neither number has a fixed scale. A sum of squares depends on the data's units and number of columns, and with two dozen columns every station is far from every other, so silhouette widths come out small even for real groups. Both need something to compare with: the same data with its groups removed. ::: {.diagram} ![Shuffling each column on its own keeps every column's values but breaks which values occur together, so the shuffled table has no groups. Clustering both tables the same way shows how much structure the observed table has beyond what any table of these values would show.](img/shuffled-baseline.svg){fig-alt="Two cards joined by an arrow labelled shuffle each column. Observed: a table of six rows and five columns, A to E, with cells shaded from white to dark blue by value; rows 1 to 3 are dark in A and B and rows 4 to 6 dark in D and E, marked by two brackets as two groups. Shuffled: the same five columns, each holding the same values in a new random order, so no rows share a pattern; each column keeps its own values, and which values occur together is lost. A note says cluster both tables the same way; only what the observed table shows beyond the shuffled one counts as structure."} ::: Shuffle each column on its own, and every column keeps exactly its own values: the same zeros, the same few large counts. Only which values occur together in a row is lost, and with it any groups. Clustering the shuffled table the same way gives a **baseline**: the scores that data like this reaches with no groups in it at all. ## Worked example ### The elbow shows no bend and the silhouette peaks at two The community matrix and the recipe are those of [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd). A function fits k-means for one $k$, and another records both measures for $k$ from 2 to 8. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax")) cluster_recipe <- function(data) { recipe(~ ., data = data) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) } fit_k <- function(data, k) { set.seed(101) workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe(data)) |> add_model(k_means(num_clusters = k) |> set_engine("stats", nstart = 25, iter.max = 100)) |> fit(data = data) } # sse_ratio is the within-cluster sum of squares as a share of the total. sweep_k <- function(data, ks = 2:8) { map_dfr(ks, \(k) { fitted <- fit_k(data, k) tibble(k = k, sse_ratio = sse_ratio(fitted)$.estimate, silhouette = silhouette_avg(fitted, new_data = data)$.estimate) }) } observed <- sweep_k(taxa_only) observed |> mutate(across(c(sse_ratio, silhouette), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| k| sse_ratio| silhouette| |--:|---------:|----------:| | 2| 0.878| 0.179| | 3| 0.779| 0.126| | 4| 0.736| 0.136| | 5| 0.707| 0.100| | 6| 0.690| 0.084| | 7| 0.676| 0.081| | 8| 0.661| 0.081|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community community = load_coastal_community() taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax") cluster_recipe = Pipeline([ ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler()), ]) def fit_k(data, k): prepared = cluster_recipe.fit_transform(data) fitted = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=25, max_iter=100, random_state=101).fit(prepared) return prepared, fitted # sse_ratio is the within-cluster sum of squares as a share of the total; # KMeans calls the within-cluster sum inertia_. def sweep_k(data, ks=range(2, 9)): rows = [] for k in ks: prepared, fitted = fit_k(data, k) total = ((prepared - prepared.mean(axis=0)) ** 2).sum() rows.append({"k": k, "sse_ratio": fitted.inertia_ / total, "silhouette": silhouette_score(prepared, fitted.labels_)}) return pd.DataFrame(rows) observed = sweep_k(taxa_only) observed.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | k | sse_ratio | silhouette | |----:|------------:|-------------:| | 2 | 0.878 | 0.179 | | 3 | 0.779 | 0.126 | | 4 | 0.736 | 0.136 | | 5 | 0.707 | 0.098 | | 6 | 0.69 | 0.083 | | 7 | 0.676 | 0.085 | | 8 | 0.662 | 0.079 | ::: ::: ::: `sse_ratio` is the within-cluster sum of squares as a share of the total, so 1 would mean no grouping at all. From $k$ = 2 to 8 it falls 0.878, 0.779, 0.736, 0.707, 0.690, 0.676, 0.661: a smooth decline with no clear bend, so the elbow gives no answer here, as it often does not on real data. The silhouette is clearer. It is highest at $k$ = 2, at 0.179. That looks small on a scale that runs to 1, and the rules of thumb in wide circulation would call anything below about 0.25 "no substantial structure". Yet [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) showed that these two clusters are the two kinds of seabed. The baseline says how to read the number. ### Shuffling each taxon gives a no-groups baseline Each taxon's counts are shuffled across the stations, separately for each taxon, and the same sweep runs on the result. One shuffle can happen to line up a few unusual values, so the shuffle is repeated five times, and the baseline is their average and range. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shuffle_columns <- function(data) { data |> mutate(across(everything(), \(x) sample(x))) } # Draw all five copies before fitting: fit_k() resets the seed. set.seed(102) copies <- map(1:5, \(i) shuffle_columns(taxa_only)) shuffles <- imap_dfr(copies, \(copy, i) sweep_k(copy) |> mutate(shuffle = i)) baseline <- shuffles |> summarise(across(c(sse_ratio, silhouette), list(mean = mean, low = min, high = max)), .by = k) baseline |> mutate(across(-k, \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| k| sse_ratio_mean| sse_ratio_low| sse_ratio_high| silhouette_mean| silhouette_low| silhouette_high| |--:|--------------:|-------------:|--------------:|---------------:|--------------:|---------------:| | 2| 0.962| 0.962| 0.963| 0.052| 0.036| 0.103| | 3| 0.929| 0.928| 0.930| 0.043| 0.039| 0.048| | 4| 0.899| 0.898| 0.900| 0.058| 0.043| 0.081| | 5| 0.870| 0.867| 0.873| 0.056| 0.051| 0.060| | 6| 0.846| 0.844| 0.849| 0.050| 0.046| 0.056| | 7| 0.822| 0.819| 0.826| 0.052| 0.047| 0.055| | 8| 0.802| 0.800| 0.804| 0.054| 0.052| 0.058|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(102) def shuffle_columns(data): return data.apply(lambda column: rng.permutation(column.to_numpy())) copies = [shuffle_columns(taxa_only) for _ in range(5)] shuffles = pd.concat([sweep_k(copy).assign(shuffle=i) for i, copy in enumerate(copies, start=1)]) baseline = shuffles.groupby("k").agg( sse_ratio_mean=("sse_ratio", "mean"), sse_ratio_low=("sse_ratio", "min"), sse_ratio_high=("sse_ratio", "max"), silhouette_mean=("silhouette", "mean"), silhouette_low=("silhouette", "min"), silhouette_high=("silhouette", "max"), ).reset_index() baseline.round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | k | sse_ratio_mean | sse_ratio_low | sse_ratio_high | silhouette_mean | silhouette_low | silhouette_high | |----:|-----------------:|----------------:|-----------------:|------------------:|-----------------:|------------------:| | 2 | 0.963 | 0.962 | 0.965 | 0.065 | 0.033 | 0.107 | | 3 | 0.931 | 0.929 | 0.933 | 0.044 | 0.041 | 0.047 | | 4 | 0.901 | 0.899 | 0.905 | 0.041 | 0.034 | 0.047 | | 5 | 0.876 | 0.873 | 0.878 | 0.045 | 0.04 | 0.052 | | 6 | 0.85 | 0.845 | 0.852 | 0.046 | 0.039 | 0.052 | | 7 | 0.827 | 0.821 | 0.83 | 0.049 | 0.045 | 0.052 | | 8 | 0.808 | 0.804 | 0.811 | 0.048 | 0.041 | 0.052 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} panel <- function(measure, label) { ggplot(lift, aes(k)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = .data[[paste0(measure, "_low")]], ymax = .data[[paste0(measure, "_high")]]), fill = ml_palette[["orange"]], alpha = 0.25) + geom_line(aes(y = .data[[paste0(measure, "_mean")]], colour = "Shuffled"), linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(aes(y = .data[[paste0(measure, "_mean")]], colour = "Shuffled"), size = 2.4) + geom_line(aes(y = .data[[measure]], colour = "Observed"), linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(aes(y = .data[[measure]], colour = "Observed"), size = 2.4) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(Observed = ml_palette[["blue"]], Shuffled = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:8) + labs(x = "number of clusters (k)", y = label, colour = NULL) } (panel("sse_ratio", "within-cluster sum of squares\n(share of total)") | panel("silhouette", "average silhouette width")) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Both measures for two to eight clusters, on the community matrix and on five shuffled copies, each taxon shuffled on its own. The band covers the five shuffles and the line is their average. The observed silhouette stands furthest above the baseline at two clusters.](choosing-the-number-of-clusters_files/figure-html/fig-k-sweep-1.png){#fig-k-sweep fig-alt='Two line charts against the number of clusters, from 2 to 8, each with an observed line and a shuffled line inside a shaded band. Left, the within-cluster sum of squares as a share of the total: both lines fall smoothly with no bend, the observed line below the shuffled one throughout, and the band is too narrow to see. Right, the average silhouette width: the shuffled average stays low, between 0.043 and 0.058, with its band widest at 2 clusters, up to 0.103; the observed line is highest at 2 clusters, at 0.179, and drops towards the baseline as k rises.' width=1800} ::: ::: ::: ### Two clusters stand furthest above the shuffled baseline On the shuffled counts, the average silhouette stays between 0.043 and 0.058 for every $k$. That is what "no groups" looks like for this measure on data of this shape. Against it, the observed 0.179 at two clusters is 3.5 times the baseline, and its lead over the baseline, 0.127, is the largest of any $k$; the next largest, at $k$ = 3, is 0.083. Even the highest of the five shuffles at two clusters reached only 0.103. The sum of squares agrees, read one step at a time. The step from one cluster to two lowers the observed share by 0.122 and the shuffled share by 0.038, a gain of 0.085 over the baseline. The step from two to three gains 0.066, and no later step gains more than 0.013. So the baseline picks two clusters, which is the hard and soft seabed. The same baseline, built by shuffling each column, comes back in [How many components to keep](dimensionality-reduction.qmd), for principal components. ## A useful number of groups is not a true one When species change gradually, as they do with depth here, there is no true number of depth groups, only a number that is useful for a purpose. A habitat map for spatial planning may need five classes because five is what a management plan can act on. That is a good reason to choose five, and not a reason to claim that five exist. Both measures here are also computed on the same data that made the clusters; [Checking a pattern before reporting it](interpreting-patterns.qmd) asks whether the clusters come back on a fresh sample. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - $k$ is an input to k-means, so the number of clusters is a choice to be made with evidence. - The **within-cluster sum of squares** always falls as $k$ rises; its **elbow** often has no clear bend. - The **silhouette width** compares each station's distance to its own cluster with its distance to the nearest other one. Its average has no fixed scale. - **Shuffling each column on its own** keeps every column's values and removes any groups, giving a **baseline** for both measures. - On the community matrix, the silhouette stood furthest above the baseline at two clusters, 3.5 times the shuffled value: the hard and soft seabed. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Shuffle the counts again with three other seeds and rerun `sweep_k()`. How much does the baseline move, and does two clusters still stand out? 2. Sweep $k$ on the survey's environmental columns (`depth_m`, `temperature_c`, `salinity_psu`, `chlorophyll_mg_m3`, rows with gaps dropped), standardised, against a shuffled copy of them. Does any $k$ stand clear of the baseline?
